healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to South Africa. Emergency numbers (10111/112), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, malaria precautions, vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.

recommended: Typhoid (for extended stays or rural travel)
Yellow Fever (required if arriving from a yellow fever endemic country)
Rabies (for animal exposure, especially dogs and wildlife)
Malaria prophylaxis (for travel to Kruger National Park and surrounding areas, and KwaZulu-Natal lowlands during summer months)
vaccinations.notes: No required vaccinations for most travelers unless arriving from a yellow fever endemic country. Malaria is a risk in Kruger National Park and some coastal areas — take prophylaxis (Larium/mefloquine, Malarone, or doxycycline). Rabies is present in some areas — avoid contact with dogs and wild animals.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open 8am-9pm; some 24-hour pharmacies in major cities; chains include Clicks, Dis-Chem Pharmacies, and independent pharmacies
pharmacy.tips: Many common medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful and knowledgeable. Bring a list of medications with generic names. Some medications may not be available — bring your supply. Malaria prophylaxis is important for certain regions.

water.notes: Tap water is generally safe to drink in major cities (Johannesburg, Cape Town, Durban). In rural areas, use bottled or filtered water as a precaution. In Cape Town, tap water is excellent. Bottled water is widely available everywhere.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: South Africa has good food safety standards in restaurants, hotels, and supermarkets. In Cape Town and major cities, restaurants maintain excellent hygiene. Be cautious with street food in informal areas. South African wine country and safari lodges maintain high standards. Avoid meat from informal vendors.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Required for visa applications but not for entry. Strongly recommended for all travelers. Medical care without insurance in private hospitals can be expensive ($1,000-5,000+/day).
travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance is strongly recommended. State hospitals are free but overcrowded. Private healthcare is excellent but expensive without insurance. Medical evacuation coverage is essential, especially for safari ( Kruger) and remote areas. Crime-related injuries are also a risk — ensure coverage includes trauma and emergency medical services.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Private healthcare in South Africa is excellent and world-class, with JCI-accredited hospitals in major cities. State hospitals are basic and overcrowded. Medical staff are well-trained. Pharmacies (Clicks, Dis-Chem, independent) are widely available. Private ambulance services (ER24, Netcare 911) are excellent but expensive.

medications.prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for prescription medications. Foreign prescriptions are not accepted — you need a South African prescription. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are Schedule 6 controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. You may need a permit from the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) for certain quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is a Schedule 5/6 substance. Some products available with prescription. Many codeine products require a prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines are controlled. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Cannabis (medical or recreational)
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in South Africa despite some decriminalization for personal use. Do not bring any cannabis products.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta)
restrictedMeds.note: Schedule 6 controlled. Bring documentation and SAHPRA permit if carrying significant quantities.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Check SAHPRA requirements if carrying Schedule 5-6 substances for extended stays.

scams.name: ATM Shoulder Surfing
scams.description: Criminals watch your PIN then follow you to steal your card.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks or malls. Cover the keypad.

scams.name: Smash and Grab
scams.description: At red lights, criminals smash windows to grab visible bags and phones.
scams.avoidance: Keep windows up, doors locked, valuables in the trunk.

scams.name: Fake Car Guards
scams.description: Unauthorized car guards demand payment, sometimes threatening damage if you don't pay.
scams.avoidance: Use secured parking lots. Small tip (R5-10) is normal for legitimate guards.

scams.name: Township Tour Scams
scams.description: Unlicensed operators take tourists to dangerous areas without proper arrangements.
scams.avoidance: Book with community-endorsed operators. Check reviews.

connectivity.simOptions: Vodacom, MTN, or Cell C prepaid SIMs at OR Tambo airport or any Pick n Pay/Checkers. Need passport. RICA registration required (done at point of sale).
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at hotels, shopping malls, and many restaurants. WiFi hotspots at some public spaces. 4G coverage good in cities, limited in rural areas.
connectivity.bestOption: Vodacom prepaid SIM for best coverage including safari areas. Buy at airport. Load shedding can affect cell towers — carry a power bank.

cultural.tipping: 10-15% at restaurants. R20-50 for car guards and gas station attendants. Tip safari guides R100-200/day per person.
cultural.dressCode: Casual. Smart casual for nice restaurants in Cape Town/Johannesburg. No specific religious dress codes.
cultural.greetings: Handshake is standard. In some cultures, a three-part handshake (clasp, grip, clasp). 'Howzit' is the informal South African greeting.
taboos: Walking alone at night in cities (safety concern, not cultural)
Flashing expensive jewelry or electronics in public
Assuming everyone speaks Afrikaans (11 official languages)
cultural.haggling: Common at craft markets and curio shops. Not at stores or restaurants. Township tours should be booked through reputable operators.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free. UK, EU also visa-free. Passport must have 2+ blank pages.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-September (dry winter — best for safari). October-November (spring, wildflowers). December-February (summer, beach weather). Cape Town: December-March.

hospitals.name: Groote Schuur Hospital
hospitals.notes: Historic hospital (site of world's first heart transplant). Public hospital with good emergency facilities.

hospitals.name: Netcare Milpark Hospital
hospitals.notes: Top private hospital in Johannesburg. Trauma center, English-speaking staff.

immediate: Monitor South African Weather Service (SAWS) storm warnings
Move vehicles to high ground during flash flood alerts
Do not cross flooded roads or low-water bridges
Follow NDMC (National Disaster Management Centre) advisories
after: Report flood damage to local municipality
Avoid contact with floodwater — disease risk
Monitor SAWS for ongoing severe weather

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 10111)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (10111) and ambulance (10177) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the LEFT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is required for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
